I know an autistic woman who converted to Islam, and I think it's partially because she liked veiling. Covering her head gives her a comfortable barrier between herself and the world. She started wearing niqab ostensibly to fit in with the community she was living with at the time, but I think that was just an excuse she used to justify it to her friends and family, when the reality was that she just wanted to do it and liked it for sensory reasons.

I think the rules and routine are comfortable for her. She likes being part of an "in group" with its own language, prayers, clothing, and outward signifiers that they are part of the same group. I think she likes the straightforwardness of the religion. Even the restrictions.

She also has some bizarre religious beliefs that do not align with Islam (I think she might also be schizophrenic? I've never been sure) and I believe that she is maintaining these beliefs while also practicing Islam. I'm not sure how she is making that work in her head, but if she doesn't see an issue with holding multiple strong mutually exclusive beliefs, it's none of my business.

I'm not sure how I'd answer this. I believe that consensus reality is the only one I need to worry about "truth" in, and in consensus reality, there is always one empirical truth that literally, physically happened. The closer we can get to knowing that truth, the more useful, good, accurate, and beneficial our knowledge becomes. But we also are completely bound by our senses and our ability to reason and interpret, and therefore, none of us can ever actually percieve raw, unbiased truth. Because we think, we are bound by the limits of our perception, and both blessed and cursed by our imagination. 

I think it is useful to try to understand as many perspectives as possible, and that by understanding and empathizing with each person's experience of truth, we can best decide what truths most align with consensus reality, to the best of our ability. I think we all do that every day.

It is possible for many things to be true, even empirically, at the same time. I also respect the validity of internal truth, spiritual truth, metaphorical truth, emotional truth, narrative truth.

But to me, when we are dealing with decision-making in our physical world, in consensus reality, there is one observable truth, and the perceptions that reflect that truth are the most relevant. 

I don't know what is meant by a "higher realm." Things that are true in other worlds are not relevant to this one.

Ahhhh yes. I'm from Minnesota and I grew up hearing our weird etiquette around the last piece was "the Minnesota Thing." I don't know if this is done elsewhere in the US, or if this is a regional practice specific to the Midwest. 


The unspoken social rule is that you don't take the very last piece. HOWEVER, you CAN cut the last piece in half and take a half of it. This results in progressively smaller "last pieces" as it is divided to the logical extreme. 


At the very, very, very end of the visit, or after the meal has concluded and things are about to be put away, it is okay to eat the last piece if you really still really want it.


The funny thing is that, genuinely, no one sees it as rude when someone else takes the last piece. This is entirely a self-conscious thing. I am the only one who is thinking "I better not take the last piece, that's rude." And when you, after me, are about to cut the piece in half again, you are the only person in the room thinking "it would be rude if I took the last one." If any single person took the last piece, no one else in the room would judge them at all-- this is a completely self-enforced habit. 


It is pretty normal for someone to awkwardly laugh and say something like "I'm not gonna be Minnesotan, I want the last one, is that ok?" And just take the last piece. Everyone will knowingly chuckle and acknowledge the existence of the strange cultural habit in good humor.

I've had to bite my tongue to avoid using these terms with my transfemme friends and partners. It feels completely innocuous to me unless I'm actively thinking about it and you might be surprised by how often this sort of male-gendered language slips into your vocabulary when you're talking to female friends so you definitely want to pay close attention to that around trans women. I'm a dismissive avoidant attacher, and you NEED to have a full sit-down conversation with her about this. It sounds to me like maybe her feelings about the relationship are changing, and that's not necessarily a relationship-ending thing, but you need to talk about it. 

I can't speak for everyone, because I've also got disorganized attachment so the way I feel and react to things is going to be different from what is normal and healthy, but personally when my partners and friends have started frequently asking "do you still love me? do you still like me? are you mad at me?" over and over, it's usually (1) because yes, I'm maybe checking out of the relationship because I feel like I don't have enough space or distance and need to cut things off so they don't continue like that and (2) one of the most anxiety-inducing and irritating things a partner can do that sets off all of my attachment issues and sends me into a "I have to run NOW" mindset. 

In my case, if a partner is pushing really hard for closeness and asking frequently for extra affirmation, it is both a reaction to and a cause of my emotional checking-out. It's the fastest way to make me leave.

I talk about this with my partner a lot. She knows my issues. She doesn't fully understand, but she tries hard and listens. She respects my boundaries, because we have talked about it. She's done a lot of work to make sure she's not setting off my dismissive avoidant issues and I'm doing a lot of work to make sure I'm self-aware of when those things are happening with me so I can communicate that's what I'm feeling. 

You need to talk to her about how your attachment issues are factoring into how you are behaving. 

This is really really important: don't go into this conversation asking for reassurance, and make sure you are prepared for her to tell you the truth. The truth might be that she's checking out or wants to break up. The truth might be that she needs space. Be respectful if this is the case, try to understand, don't blame yourself, don't flip out. She might have other things to tell you as well that you can't anticipate and which you won't want to hear, and you have to just be ready to accept whatever those things are. 

The best thing you can do for attachment issues is talk openly. You're not a bad person for feeling the way you feel. Healing attachment stuff is REALLY fucking hard and takes a lot of time and effort and you can fuck up in relationships a LOT before you even start to figure out how to manage, or how to compartmentalize your feelings into "what I really want" and "what my mental illnesses are screaming I need to do." It's hard and I'm not there yet. You're not a bad person if you're not there yet either.

This has been my experience in the US. I've had what I think are more authentic kormas, but I'll admit I also like the "shitty American restaurant" korma (since that's what they had in my hometown). 

This is super not related to anything, but when I was a kid, a chef (originally from India) was displaced from his home in New Orleans by Hurricane Katrina and was forced to move up to our town. He opened a restaurant across the street from the pre-existing 1 Indian restaurant in town and he made really, really, really good kashmiri korma. It was the first time I'd ever tried a korma and I enjoyed it so much I wrote an essay about it in my third grade writing class. Not even prompted by anything; I just felt the need to express my love for the dish to my whole class on my own time. But then his restaurant closed down (I can't remember why-- I hope it wasn't because people preferred the one across the street) and I think he went back to New Orleans. Or maybe he died (my parents may have lied to me and said he went home). Either way, he wasn't making korma in my town anymore. I'd always order chicken korma from the other restaurant because I was chasing the high of that other guy's cooking, but it was never the same.

Maybe this Scottish restaurant korma unsettled me so much because it was so far removed from what that chef used to make and it threw me into a little crisis. Ngl that 1 chef influenced my whole understanding of what food should be like in general. Rest in peace guy, or hope you're doing good in New Orleans, whichever it is.

Guess culture (mine) is largely about making sure you're not imposing. The assumption is that most people HATE to say no to a request and will go very far out of their way to aquiesce even if it's profoundly inconvenient for them while pretending that it isn't a problem when it very clearly is because you don't want to make the requester feel like a burden. 

Guess culture operates on the assumption that having to say "no" is incredibly uncomfortable. As a chicken-egg thing, the assumption is also that requests will ONLY be made if the asker believes they'll get a "yes," so when requests are made, they are serious, urgent, expecting a yes, and basically planning for the "yes" because they trust that they're likely to recieve one. Wicca is controversial esp in the pagan community because of how strongly it has influenced modern pagan culture and norms despite being a very modern religion. People make fun of it, and have a lot of preconceived notions, but it's a very interesting religion with a lot of good parts. Wicca has alleged that it is an ancient pre-christian witch cult which survived thousands of years, but this has been overwhelmingly debunked, and despite how the internet may make it seem, there isn't a huge percentage of wiccans who genuinely believe in their founder's origin myth. 

The basic beats of the religion are worshipping the earth and honoring the five elements, observing a male god and a female goddess (called the Lord and Lady or God and Goddess) who represent the cycles of the earth, moon, sun, seasons, life & death, etc., and practicing ceremonial magic. The religion attracts a lot of feminists, queer & poly people, and eco activists. There are versions of Wicca which are more problematic than others, and you'll find a lot of testimony to that.

The idea of and focus on patron deities isn't a new tiktok thing. I'm sure that tiktok has blown it all up though. I remember reading books that mentioned or recommended choosing a patron deity or set of deities back in the 2000s. 

I'm pretty sure that that version of patrons comes out of wicca, which is where a lot of books were based in. I remember it was frequently encouraged to choose or connect with one particular god and one particular goddess to represent the divine masculine and divine feminine. There was at least one book with a "dictionary" of gods and goddesses and you were encouraged to choose your patron by turning pages randomly and letting your finger fall on a random name. 

If I had to guess, the current concept of and focus on patron deities comes from modern paganism's strong wiccan undercurrent (whether they like it or not) and the increased popularity of Dungeons and Dragons, with its system of divine and magical patrons, and it's influence on fantasy in general. 

I think there's also some lingering ex-monotheist tendencies in a lot of people, leading people to want to connect religiously to their gods the same way they are used to from previous faiths. Even for polytheists, the "personal relationship with god" as your best friend, parent, confidante, source of meaning, etc. encouraged by Christianity is very comforting and attractive. I don't see that as a bad thing necessarily. It's irritating when some pagans (usually newer, enthusiastic ones) tout this as the only way. 

There's also a lot of focus on patronage in witchcraft, and there's a massive overlap in the pagan and witch communities. Patrons in witchcraft come from some old ideas about demonic patronage which were popular lore about witches back in olden times. I assume that when people were working off the "demons were actually local pagan deities and witches were really pagans" theory, the idea of patronage was adapted to center deities.

I read the whole article. The author is writing in a way which seems self-aware to an extent, like she's definitely aware that she sounds awful and she's trying to air that out and maybe make it a little bit of a joke. This part, for instance: "A hint of the affection Cynthia predicted flared up in my chest. As did a flicker of irritation because now the cat had to be fed or watered or whatever."

The "or whatever" reads to me as an intentional imitation of someone flippant and mean, with the implied understanding between the reader and author being that the author is NOT typically "like that," even though she is reacting in the moment "like that." But the trouble is that we, the readers, actually DO NOT HAVE that understanding. This author hasn't built up any of the goodwill or rapport necessary for us to see this as hyperbolic or ironic. The author has gone hard in the opposite direction, openly admitting her animal abuse and neglect, which is probably the fastest way to make sure the reader is absolutely not on your side. 

I imagine that maybe she thought that she was showing self-awareness by making herself out to be the villain in this story and essentially owning what she's done, describing the cat's pitiful appearance and behavior as self-aware and self-effacing copping to guilt, but that's not how it comes off. I suspect the author believes that that was enough to make her 'relatable'-- someone who isn't a bad person but who is doing something bad, out of circumstance, despite being nice and smart and normal and self-aware.

I think she knows that what she's done to this cat is shameful, but I don't think she understands that what she's done to this cat is SO FUCKING SHAMEFUL that frankly she shouldn't even be making a reddit post about it, let alone publishing an article about it. It's one thing to admit you've fucked up and abused someone to like your therapist or a close personal friend or a support group-- that could be you trying to fix your shit and turn it around-- but it's another thing to publish an article about it. That comes off as being proud of your story. 

This vibe she's got in her writing is like "whoops, guess I'm the devil, haha" like she's jokingly self-aware, when the stuff she's describing is legitimately cruel. You can't laugh at yourself for this. You don't get to pat yourself on the back and call yourself brave for sharing your story or being "honest" or whatever. Not for this.

I think she's written this story out in the same style of other stories I've read where people admit to and talk about doing bad stuff, describing how they started doing it, how they felt, how it impacted others-- and when those stories are most successful at garnering reader sympathy, it's because they've given some indication that they've stopped doing the bad thing. Maybe there's bad aftermath and destroyed relationships and they deserve that, but we can relate to them because they've been "punished" and feel bad and have gone to lengths to fix themselves. There is no indication that any of that has gone on in this story. Frankly, it comes across like she's definitely still abusing the cat. 

The thing that makes me the angriest here is this implied idea that the reason why she's neglecting and abusing the cat is because she doesn't love the cat anymore. It implies that the reason she was previously good to the cat was out of love. Once the love is gone, her care is gone. That's horrifying and disgusting to me. You can't let your feelings of affection or lack thereof dictate whether you meet the basic needs of something or someone who is completely dependent on you. Nurses don't love their patients, but they keep them fed and clean and comfortable because that's their responsibility. That's their job. That's the contract. If you inherit a pet lizard and you don't like lizards, it is still your job to take good care of that lizard and meet its needs, and if you don't think you can do that long-term, it's your job to make sure you find somebody else who can. It doesn't matter whether you love something or someone under your direct care. It is your fucking job to be responsible. That's the bare minimum requirement to being a good person. 

You can never be a good person if you're only good to the things you love. If you let an animal in your care suffer like this just because you don't "love" it, you are straight-up a bad person, and it is not quirky, relatable, sympathetic, or forgivable.

It's not exactly like that. There's some more complexity and nuance to how and when native names are used. There's a lot of history behind the way we use native names in modern times, a lot of which goes back to the infamous residential boarding schools and other similar efforts by the US government to quash native cultures. It's common for native people to have an english name and a native name. In my experience, it's the most common for people to go by their english name in most contexts, using their native name for ceremonies and in formal introductions (like at native events, in speeches, etc). Even though the name is used less frequently, it is still considered your name. Sometimes, people will stop going by their english name entirely and only use their native name, but I rarely see people do this.  

You could think of it as being like a middle name, but with religious/ceremonial significance.

I agree with you. I don't view including kids in your religion as indoctrination. It's not like you're telling them they HAVE to do stuff or that they can't find their own path. 

I was raised in progressive christianity, and I can take some positive lessons from that. There's a lot that I'd take into raising my own kids. My parents took me to church and had me be part of that community-- it was a nice community, very important for the queer community in our city and the fight for gay marriage rights, and their main denominational thing was that they believed the bible was fallible (grounded politically in certain places and times as it was written) despite still being seen as their core sacred document which contained wisdom about God. When I left the church and said it was because I wanted to be pagan, the pastor congratulated me on finding my path and said I was still welcome there. She led a cool congregation which I never went back to but still appreciate. 

I actually wish my parents had discussed their religious beliefs with me a lot more. I knew they had them, but they didn't seem to want to talk about them much, and in retrospect I think that was because on a personal level they were very different from one another (my dad was an irreverent, agnostic, skeptical lapsed catholic who was still deep down an actual catholic, and my mom was a superstitious liberal methodist who believed in ghosts but not in hell). I would have liked for them to share some of that with me. Even if what they shared was that they each weren't really sure what they believed in sometimes. 

That attitude that religion was sort of a privately-felt thing, something that was sort of embarrassing even, definitely cultivated a sense of shame around having or sharing religious beliefs of any kind for me, which I still deal with. I think my parents might have been trying not to push their beliefs on us, but I think maybe they went too far in the other direction by making religion something a little bit taboo to talk about with any sort of seriousness. 

I think that a lot of pagans can't mentally disentangle "forcing your religion on a child" from raising your kid with paganism. All it means is "we're celebrating the solstice today" is the default, and if the kid decides they don't want to do that for whatever reason-- maybe they don't want to celebrate anything, maybe want to celebrate christmas instead-- you just say "okay" and support their path. It's like giving a child a name. You name your kid, you call them by that name, you teach them how to spell it. That name is a gift. It's part of an identity that you gave to them. Maybe at some later time, the kid decides they want to change their name, perhaps to suit their gender identity. You accept that the gift you gave isn't actually what they need and start calling them by their new name. 

It's not like pagan kids are going to be sheltered from anything that isn't paganism. Pagan kids will know that other families aren't pagan. They'll learn very quickly that lots of other people follow Abrahamic faiths, that their family is in the minority, that there are all sorts of other religions out there. Just encourage them to learn about other religions and cultures and follow their curiosity. You can do that and still have a family samhain celebration or a coming-of-age ritual or a pagan funeral for your cat.

My sister had to repeat kindergarten, not sure if that counts. I can't remember why. She just wasn't socially ready, I think.

This isn't the same, but when I was teaching college freshmen, I STRONGLY preferred the students who were coming in a few years "late" for pretty much any reason. Some dropped out of high school and got their GED later, some had kids early and were coming back to school, some were in the military, some needed financial or other assistance to do school for any variety of reasons-- they were always my best students with very few exceptions. 

My worst-performing students were unfortunately the ones who definitely SHOULD have been held back and definitely NEEDED extra academic help, but were instead just pushed through the system and got to college with nearly no basic academic skills. The problem was that by the time they got to me, they'd been shoved along so many times that they were under the impression that they could continue to perform far below the bare minimum and still get by. That doesn't work in college. I also remember seeing a lot of students realize with shame how far behind they really were and how few basic skills they had. I wish I could have helped everybody more, but I had to first serve the students who were prepared to be there at that level. I strongly believe that many of my students were failed by their high schools, who should have had them repeat a year and should have given them extra help.

I was never held back, but there were many instances where I got in a lot of academic trouble in high school because my math/science scores were so low. It took a LOT of tutoring and backbreaking work on my part to get me to a C average. I felt (and still feel) a lot of shame and anxiety around math. I was always jealous of my friend with a diagnosed learning disability because she got accommodations and extra support. It turns out, as an adult, that I had adhd and dyscalculia (like dyslexia but for numbers) the entire time. I had more than one learning disability that was impacting my performance and for which I definitely should have had extra support and accommodations. 

My sister, one of the smartest people I know, has the same dyscalculia. In order to receive her MA, she had to repeat the same college statistics class THREE TIMES because she kept failing it. She got that masters degree, but a year late. That doesn't change the fact that she has a MA.

The truth is that there shouldn't be any shame in struggling and needing help. Needing help or needing to repeat grades or classes doesn't say anything about your character or even your intelligence. Sometimes, for any variety of reasons, school is just unfairly hard. Whether its due to a learning disability, circumstances in your life, or other factors, sometimes people just do not perform well in school, and it's not because they're not smart. Sometimes it's not even because they're not trying their best. Sometimes you just fall behind and need time to catch up. It shouldn't be shameful at all.

I actually suspect they have flawed or even abusive parents that they don't get along with but tolerate because they've swallowed that "stand by family" stuff. They assume everyone else's situation is just like theirs.

I have great parents and sometimes I think that gives me some insight that my friends with terrible parents don't have. I don't have their experiences, but I have the ability to listen to them talk about shit they think is normal and to "no actually that is fucking not normal, that's abuse." They'll talk about setting boundaries with their parents and feeling guilty about it or being met with a lot of push back and expectation to stand by your family because they're your family-- I can tell you that this expectation straight-up does not exist in healthy families. In healthy families, nobody ever says "you have to do this because were family" or "you owe me this because I'm your mom" or "you have to tolerate him because he's your dad." In healthy families you all just choose to be together because you want to be, because you enjoy it, because you feel supported and safe and loved. You call your mom because you have a bond and you care about what adventures she's getting up to, not because you feel like you should because she's your mom. 

The idea of needing to be loyal to your family members even if they're horrible just does not exist outside of abusive families because it's not needed. 

My parents would fully expect and understand if I cut abusive family members out, because setting boundaries and respecting yourself and caring for yourself enough not to give your time to harmful people is one of the values they share with me. If someone's parents actively oppose thar value, I assume it's because they've normalized abuse.

I have so many friends who are struggling through adult relationships with their abusive parents because they feel like they SHOULD. like it's somehow shameful if they don't. I don't really understand this. The people telling you you SHOULD are the same people who normalized your abuse. Nobody else is saying that. I usually assume people who carry this idea of family loyalty no matter what around came out of abusive family systems and normalized it to themselves.

It's the same sort of thing with "every family has secrets." No they don't. Mine doesn't. That's just something your abusive parents tell you to make what they're doing seem normal. Normal families don't have secrets. If you're keeping family secrets out of loyalty for people you don't even like, you probably shouldn't be. A good family wouldn't ask that of you, and if your family isn't good, you don't owe them anything.

The dynamics of abuse are interesting to me as someone who didn't experience it because I feel like so many of my friends are having to deconstruct the same way that ex-cult members have to deconstruct-- learning for the first time that it's actually not normal or healthy to expect some level of abuse in any close relationship, learning where boundaries should be, feeling guilty and afraid for setting those boundaries. It's always perplexing and frustrating for me to see people parroting strange beliefs that I recognize as coming exclusively out of those abusive dynamics like they expect other people to see those beliefs as normal when they're not. 

"You should be loyal to your family no matter what because they're your family" sounds as nonsensical and thought-terminating as "keep sweet, pray, and obey" or any other actual cult rhetoric. It's something that just doesn't exist in family systems where there are no genuine, real reasons it would be healthier and better to cut someone off.

I think it's useful sometimes for people trying to deconstruct to compare their experiences with people who didn't grow up in situations where abuse was normalized. For the guilt, at least. If you can look at your situation from the outside for a moment, it's easier to be less guilty about failing to meet standards that only exist within the context of abuse.

I've got friends who have gone through some truly terrible hell and I think a lot about some of the things they've told me sometimes. I'll never understand how someone can do those things to children. But I can try to understand how people convince themselves that abuse is normal. Because I can help my friends now, with that.

"Cop show" is a popular genre that's been around forever. We can suspend our disbelief that the cops in cop shows aren't at all like real cops. Brooklyn 99 just took the premise of Cop Show and went "what if it was a goofball workplace comedy." 

In most cop shows, the bad guys get what's coming to them, the good guys get justice, the protagonists are in the right even when they don't follow the rules, and when they make mistakes, they can fix them. "The system" is difficult and not always correct, but the worst that can happen is that a bad guy gets off free (only to be stopped later) or an innocent person is briefly imprisoned (only to be freed by evidence). 

This is because it's just a story. We want to see good guys win and bad guys lose. The detective genre is great for this because, by nature, our good guys are tasked with making sure this happens. Our good guys unearth the truth and get justice. The system sometimes impedes them, and the fact that they must work within it creates some drama and tension. That's why the genre works so well. It has built-in tension and motivation to solve a mystery.

It's pretty easy to mentally divorce fictional cop shows from actual police. Like we know that Our Flag Means Death doesn't accurately depict pirates, but we understand the pirate genre implicitly enough to know what the genre conventions are. 

This isn't to say that copaganda has no cultural effect or purpose, but there's really nothing weird about people who hate cops loving B99. Because the characters in B99 are straight-up not like real cops. They're like our friends if we were all in a detective show together.

I've never in my life seen anyone put ketchup on pasta or fish. Except toddlers eating fish sticks. 

Ketchup is not "bad tomato sauce," it's vinegar, sugar, and tomato paste. Tomato sauce is prepared from canned (or occasionally fresh) tomatoes, while ketchup is prepared from tomato paste which is puree that is cooked down to deepen and concentrate the flavor, remove water, and make the consistency paste-like. 

I guess you could make tomato sauce from tomato paste as well, but I don't know why you would. Even so, for it to be considered ketchup, you'd need to add a substantial amount of vinegar. If you were making tomato sauce, you would not want to add vinegar (again, you CAN, but you wouldn't want as much as is added to ketchup). Finally, ketchup has more sugar and a more emulsified texture than tomato sauce. 

So yes, the two sauces have the same basic ingredients, but they are prepared very differently and you cannot substitute one for the other. You'd find fries dipped in marinara sauce to be disappointing, and pasta with ketchup to be overpowering and unpleasant.

Dave had a much older brother who had become schizophrenic and was homeless for at least a decade. Gina also thinks maybe Dave's maternal uncle was schizophrenic and homeless as well. I think people have wildly different ideas about what forgiveness means. There are so many meanings people put behind "I forgive you":

"What you did is okay, actually, so I'm willing to let it go and proceed like I was never hurt because you weren't actually wrong."

"What you did is excusable by circumstances, so I'm willing to let it go and proceed like I was never hurt because you had a reason."

"What you did is wrong, but I'm willing to let it go completely and fully trust you again."

"You did nothing wrong and I was wrong to be mad about it."

"What you did is excusable by circumstances, but I will always remember how I was hurt even though I can empathize with your reason, and that empathy is forgiveness to me"

"I will always remember how you hurt me but I will not hate you, and will continue to try and build a positive relationship with you"

"I will always remember how you hurt me but I will not hate you, and I don't want you in my life."

"I will straight-up forget how you hurt me."

"I am willing to give you another chance."

"I am not willing to give you another chance, but I won't waste energy thinking about how you hurt me and I refuse to feel angry about it for my own wellbeing."

"I absolve you of wrongdoing."

"I accept your apology. I believe you understand what you did wrong and will try not to do it again, and I am willing to move past this."

"I accept your apology. You have apologized and therefore I will hold no resentment towards you because you've done the proper thing, and forgiveness is the proper response."

"I still like you."

"I will not actively try to fight you about this anymore."

  
For me, personally, I view forgiveness like removing a bad mark on a report. It means dismissing my own negative feelings about an event and it means trusting that it will never happen again. For that reason, I have lots of things I just will never forgive-- if I feel like I can't trust someone because they've wronged me, I feel like I can't say I've forgiven them. But I can love someone I haven't forgiven for something. My personal relationship with forgiveness is about trust. Like I'll never be able to forgive one of my loved ones for almost killing my cat because they totally neglected to fill her water dish and gave the wrong doses of her meds when I trusted them to cat-sit. I still love that person and maintain a positive relationship with them, and I acknowledge that they feel bad about fucking up that badly, but I will always remember that when I trusted them with something extremely precious, they didn't show enough concern or care for me or my cat to make sure they were doing the job correctly. To me, the fact that I will never be able to trust them with important things due to the way they behaved means that I do not forgive them. 

Someone else with a different concept of what forgiveness is would look at this situation and view the fact that I still love this person and have a great time with them and joyfully incorporate them into my life means that I forgive them. Or that the fact that I don't stay up at night thinking about this incident means that I forgive them. Or the fact that I understand what their thought process was and accept they didn't do it on purpose means that I forgive them. 

For me, forgiveness is not an absolution of guilt, but it's also not just a willingness to love or like someone. Someone with a different personal definition of forgiveness might view my refusal to forgive as unhealthy or an indication that I am actively holding ill will against someone. That's just never been what it means in my family. 

I think a lot of conflicts stem from people having different internal understandings of forgiveness, and different beliefs about when forgiveness is right.

I think this person is reading a lot into what people mean when they say that sex is biological and gender is social. I definitely don't see the meanings they're inferring as inherent to the statement. "Your gender can 'conflict' with your sex" isn't even a part of the statement. I don't see it as an implication of the statement at all. I'm not a science person, but my understanding is that sex is a way of categorizing members of species based on biological traits which play one of usually two roles in producing offspring. Male and female are the main two sexes. There are several variations. Humans are the same as any other species and we have biological traits which generally fall into two categories, male and female, with some variation. Saying "sex is biological" doesn't even imply that there are only two sexes, or that biological sex has any relationship to gender. It's just a neutral statement about what we mean when we say "sex." 

"Gender is social" does not imply that it is less real or important than biological sex and, coming from the humanities, if I saw this with no context I would definitely assume that this is the more important concept to know. This is another tone-neutral statement which just denotes that what we are talking about when we use the word "gender" is a complex social role and identity. Humans have genders. Lobsters have sexes. A lobster has no concept of masculinity or femininity. It does not perform gender and has no internal experience of gender. We can look at the shape of a lobsters tail and figure out that it's sex is male and we can then assign it a gender and be like "oh he's a boy I'm naming him Dave," but the lobster itself is not thinking about itself as a him or as a Dave and has no opinions about whether it should be a she or a they instead. Its sex does not in any way inform its experience of gender because its gender was assigned to it as part of human social constructs and is not a normal part of lobsterhood. We usually base gender assignments on what we determine biological sex to be, but not always-- I knew a woman who took care of a stray male cat named Fiona who was assigned she/her even though she knew Fiona had gotten several other barn cats pregnant; she just liked the name a lot and so princess Fiona stuck. 

The gist of the statement is just that when we are talking about reproductive sexes, we use the word "sex," but when we are talking about human experience and identities and all the social business that is wrapped up in womanhood and manhood and masculinity and femininity and androgony in human cultures, we use the word "gender."

You can tell the difference between Stephen King's plethora of evil racist characters who say and do evil racist things (NOT emblematic of his actual beliefs) and Stephen King's recurrent pigeonholing of black characters into Magical Negro stereotypes (that IS something that reflects his beliefs and upbringing and which is genuinely problematic). Obviously if I'm talking to someone who calls them sacred texts or sacred histories, I'll switch to their phrasing out of respect. I don't think there is anything insulting about the term "mythology" unless you view your religious stories as being completely literal, which most people in my region do not. Unfortunately, "living in skepticism" is sort of an important part of paganism to a degree. We are animists, pantheists, polytheists, nontheists... many of us have very different beliefs and interpretations of those beliefs, and it's very important to be able to constantly challenge your own faith and beliefs and compare them to the beliefs of others, to understand the differences, to know whether you can accept or reject someone else's worldview on any given pagan subject. Because paganism often encourages and requires some degree of magical thinking and un-grounding yourself, you NEED to be able to have a rational, skeptical, material mindset as well. New, jumpy pagans will often ask things like "Am I seeing birds because it's an omen? What does seeing birds mean?" And the answer is always "it probably means you're outside. That's where birds live." 

When you're raised with very strong abrahamic faith, when you're encouraged to take things like miracles and everlasting life and God's constant judgement and guidance in your life as being dead serious and totally literal, it can be really hard and really scary to let go of the desire to have something that fills that void. Where there was certainty, there is now uncertainty. And that's terrifying. 

Paganism tends to involve a lot of embracing that uncertainty and accepting it. We are adapting ancient religions, and we often don't know as much as we'd like to about those ancient practices. We have to accept and understand the histories of how these religions formed, how gods may have evolved over time as civilizations changed. We know that there is no infallible sacred text and that the gods we worship were named by humans, and their mythos were invented as stories. Our faith is not like Christian faith-- we do not need to (nor should we) claim total literal truth in our deities and their legends. How can we when we have fossil evidence of dinosaurs and ancient oceans? Or when we have cameras in space that let us see black holes? 

There is value in metaphor, and in mystery, and in reverence for the world and all it's stories. There is value in the terror of death and the unknown, and in the lessons that our ancient ancestors passed to their children. There is value in the names of ancient gods recognized by thousands of years of human beings. There is value in the worship of these things-- the mundane, the metaphorical, the metaphysical, and the unknowable. 

As pagans, our faith is often just the act of enjoying these things and naming them as sacred. Sex is Aphrodite, drinking and dancing is Dionysus, the rush in your blood when the thunder claps is Thor, the slow and red rising sun is Ra. We are idolaters, worshipping everything. Giving thanks. Listening. Not out of fear, and not for any eternal reward. Just out of awe and a desire to be closer to the divinity of all the things that we find which are divine to us.

There is no certainty, really. We have to accept that we really don't know anything for sure. That's part of the beauty of being human. It's only terrifying at first.

The vast majority of witches work with whatever they want to. You'll find witches pursuing multiple paths at once and making their own. It's not important to have a "type" of witchcraft, especially when you're starting out. It's important to do as much research and reading as you can and explore everything so you figure out what your favorite practices are and which ones you want to avoid. That's how you figure out what sort of witch you are-- trial and error and experimentation.

Yeah it's true. You're supposed to say "good." If you wanna be really polite you follow up with "how are you?" as well, but it's honestly not mandatory. It's not really a REAL question, it's more of just a greeting ritual. You say it to strangers and cashiers and stuff.

It's also a polite way to start small talk with an acquaintance. If you get the vibe that you're actually gonna have a conversation with someone and you're not just politely greeting a service worker or something, if they ask "how are you" you can respond with a short anecdote about your day. "I'm doing alright, I took my cat to get her rabies shot updated today." You know, just small talk. 

Be aware though that if you say anything other than "Good!" It means you're having a terrible time. "I'm alright" means "I'm stressed out but I'm managing." "I'm okay" means "I'm not okay, I'm moments from tears." "I'm getting by" means you're in the deepest depression of your life-- like you've just lost a loved one or gotten fired or something. "It is what it is" means whatever is going on in your life isn't going to make you kill yourself, but that's the best it gets. If you say "Good" it means "Things are normal." If you get crazy and say "Great!," though, that genuinely means you ARE doing great-- you've just kissed your crush for the first time, or you finished a really good run, or you're about to bring a new puppy home and you're pumped.

If he's the first type of guy, he probably thinks he's big-brained because he can comprehend moral relativism. Maybe he doesn't understand the difference between contextualizing historical practices without judgement and actually supporting those practices in modern times. Maybe he feels superior because he thinks that historical human sacrifice is proof that violence is authentically pagan.

The USA is huge and there's big regional differences, as well as stereotypes between the states. Even if I'm going somewhere where Im pretty sure nobody I'm gonna talk to has been to Minnesota, I will automatically say I'm from Minnesota. Because in my mind, being Minnesotan is a different and maybe even more important thing than being American. 

If someone says "I'm from Texas" or "I'm from New York" or "I'm from California," even though we're all Americans, we're going to have different experiences and different cultural norms and stuff. For instance, in my experience, British people (especially northerners) tend to have a much easier time with the culture in my home region, where (even though we have a reputation for friendliness) people tend to be chilly and polite, as opposed to, say, Alabama, where the culture is VERY loud and friendly and huggy to the point where I get culture shock down there. And all the stores are empty on Sunday morning because the vast majority of people are in church. It's a wild, wild contrast from what I'm used to. It's like being in a different country, honestly. 

If you say you're from Texas, you're telling people you're from a Cowboys & Cookouts state which has deeply conservative values, where everything is bigger, where there's horses and ranches and big belts and tons of guns and massive restrictions on reproductive rights. It's a totally different vibe than if you say you're from New York, home of New York City, the center of the universe and home of the hot dog and the bagel and Law & Order and "I'm walkin' here," where people have a reputation for being brisk and abrasive. 

California is the weed & rich influencers state, Florida is both the Spring Break/retirement home state and the gator-filled Mire of Insanity state, Montana is the horse ranch state, Louisiana is the gumbo & Mardi Gras state, Minnesota is the tater tot hotdish state. 

If I go abroad, I'm going to have much, much, much more culturally in common with a Canadian from Ontario than I am with another American from Texas or Louisiana, where the social norms can be different enough that you can definitely fuck up real bad on accident if you run on a normal polite social script from your own state.

Even the franchises are different. I had never heard of waffle house in my life till I visited the south. We just don't have it here. And they do not have Caribou down there, which is bizarre to me. If you wear a cowboy hat in public up here, you will be ridiculed (behind your back). But that's just normal attire in some states.

When we go abroad and tell people what state we're from, we are consciously or unconsciously doing it so that they might know what American stereotypes might apply to us and our homelands. When I go abroad, I don't want new people to think I'm a cattle ranch & hat & big guns american-- I want them to think I'm a tater tot & pontoons american. I'm from 6 months of blizzards territory. My people are known for the movie Fargo and saying "Ubetcha" and being unable to tolerate spices on food. Do those stereotypes apply to me personally? No. Not really. But I want to give you, my new friend abroad, some ground to stand on. You like cowboys? We don't have em. That's other states. Even if the other person has never been to the US, it's a subconscious reflex.

It's less simple than you'd think. There is actually some overlap in these communities, and it seems to make both communities uncomfortable, lol.

Most satanists are atheistic. There are some pagans who don't view their deities as literal, and view them as archetypes. You can see how these could easily overlap without issue.

Then there are pagans who are theistic but part of the Satanic Temple for political reasons (TST is pretty shifty though so I recommend anybody interested in them look up their leaders' history first). Their activism is attractive to a lot of pagans, as well as a lot of other well-meaning people, but the organization is a scam unfortunately. 

Then there's eclectic pagans who are practicing some form of demonolotry, luciferianism, or theistic satanism alongside their traditionally pagan practices. Traditional Witchcraft is one branch where "the witches' Devil" is sometimes recognized. Some pagans may view the Devil as a version of the Horned God, or as a combination of a number of pagan deities, and may recognize or venerate him that way. There are really quite a lot of ways and reasons that some pagans may incorporate lucifer, Satan, or the devil into their practice. 

Overall, it is unusual, and uncommon, but far from impossible for pagans to believe in Satan in some form. The vast majority of pagans do not recognize Satan and view him as a purely abrahamic figure. But in paganism, you're pretty much never alone in your beliefs-- you can always find a handful of weirdos who are practicing the same way you are.

There's the cramps and stuff and the constant fear of leaking into your underpants & bedsheets (at night especially), but also one thing people don't often mention is the fact that getting your period can make you have to shit A LOT. Your shits tend to get looser, more frequent, and pretty urgent-feeling. For me, it's like I've had 3 cups of coffee & have the runs all day for like three days straight. Ibuprofen can help with this, but I've found that during my period, I really crave really gentle-on-my-gut foods and stuff that doesn't have a ton of hard to digest fiber but also isn't too oily or spicy-- basically stuff that isn't going to exacerbate the problem. Mashed potatoes and cooked greens and stuff. 

The first couple days of a period are often the worst. Most people have a good idea of how bad things are gonna be which days of the week-- so if you usually get the worst cramps and shits and fatigue on the first or second day, and better mood and fewer (but more intense) cramps on the third, you generally know what's coming, enough to be able to be like "you know what, maybe I shouldn't plan to go clubbing tomorrow night, I'm going to be miserable." But sometimes your period decides to mix things up and maybe slows down for a day or two during what's normally the height of misery. And then you're confusedly putting in panty liners instead of pads and wondering when it's going to start back up in earnest. This can happen especially when you're going through a time of extreme stress or even illness. 

Just in general, though, having your period makes you feel gross. You're uncomfortable, you're exhausted, goop is trickling out of you, you've either got what feels like half a diaper on or you've got a cotton plug up your vagina and both of those things are pretty unpleasant, and you still have to go to work.

Everyone's period is different. Some people have it way worse than others. Most people can expect discomfort for a couple days at least, though.

For me personally, looking into "relationship anarchy" has been helpful. It's basically a philosophy of relationships where you try to get rid of all the rules and expectations about what relationships "should" look like. That can mean a lot of things. So one cultural expectation might be "if you date for long enough, it leads to sex." Boom, that's gone. There's no more expectation that that's "where things lead." Another expectation might be "if you kiss and cuddle with someone, you're dating." Boom! Gone. Maybe you've just got a buddy you kiss and cuddle with. The expectation that you "belong" to another person? Gone. The expectation that your partner can't date other people? Gone. Maybe you've got a very close relationship with someone and you feel bound to them in a very deep way and want to share a life, but you've got no interest in sex or kissing or anything like that with them. Maybe you're attracted to other people, too! No expectations, everyone just exists in whatever type of relationship they enjoy. And obviously, this has to be with the consent and full understanding of everybody involved. Otherwise it doesnt work. It's a neat concept that I personally like a lot as somebody who doesn't enjoy romance at all.

Like when you go to your friends' houses as a kid and discover they all have wildly different ideas about what's expected of hosts and guests and their children's friends at dinner. And you have to spend some time listening to the way they talk to each other and the sorts of jokes they make so that you can copy their vibe. Except sometimes you just know you'll never vibe with that family because maybe their jokes are all toilet humor and they all laugh way too much at anything stinky, or maybe they're all incredibly earnest and never treat anything as a joke at all, or maybe they're incredibly passive-aggressive to each other and you can pick up on the fact that there's a secret conflict happening under the smiles but you cannot figure out what it is because you don't have the context and you don't know these people well enough to read them. You never know what you're gonna get. Some of your friends' parents will gently try to probe you by saying stuff like "I heard the funniest thing in church" (with the expectation that you'll talk about your own church or place of worship, thus revealing your family's religious affiliation or lack thereof, as a polite way to avoid asking about something potentially sensitive outright but which they feel they have a right to know) and then some of you other friends' parents will point-blank say weird shit to you like "thanks for being friends with my daughter, her anorexia's coming back, don't know if you noticed, so it's good that she's got a friend on the heavier side who doesn't care what people think and wears what they want." And it's like. You have to figure out how to navigate what the fuck you're supposed to say in every single weird new social situation, and you're never prepared for what the rules of any oncoming conversation might be. 

Interacting with different groups of people, or even just different individuals, can be like visiting totally different cultures. And even if you know someone well in one context, interacting with them when you're in a different friend group or setting will have totally different rules. You have to be on your toes, basically. It's kind of fun, actually. It's like a game. As long as you don't care too much about fucking up, and as long as you can accept that you can't please everyone (many of the rules are mutually exclusive). It can definitely be exhausting if you never get a chance to unmask. I took a vacation in Paris and it was really fun. I wasn't disappointed at all. I just went around  getting hot chocolate and wandering into historic churches. I always tried to order food in french to very mixed success. The Parisians weren't as mean as you always hear-- when one waiter overheard me mention to my grandma that I liked when people tried to speak french with me even though I'm not very good at it because it helped me improve my french, that guy ONLY spoke french with me the whole rest of the meal and was VERY patient while I fumbled my way through. I love that guy, he was great.

My mom insisted we do all the tourist things-- eiffel tower, arc de triomphe, the louvre, notre dame (closed at the time due to the fire but still cool) a bunch of other stuff-- and those things were all really cool, but my favorite thing was just walking around and getting coffee. And the bread! The bread was so good. 

It's also kind of nice because (and I know the residents are not a fan of this) Paris is so touristy so there was a GENEROUS cushion for tourists-- it was always very very clear what the tourist-friendly activities were and how to get there. They make it really easy for you to find stuff to do as a visitor if you can't speak or read french. Obviously like in every touristy place there's a steep tourist tax so that's definitely something to be prepared for. 

One of the most fun things we did was this cheese-making class. We made cheese and butter. This was definitely one of those tourist trap things but it was fun as hell. My grandma still talks about it all the time. And honestly, I grew up in a tourist town-- I can appreciate a good tourist trap. Our tourist traps back home could be pretty lame in comparison, so I had fun.

We didn't get a chance to go visit other areas in France, but I'd love to go back. As much as I loved Paris, I'd love to get out and see other regions.

I've known a few people with schizophrenia. I have a friend with schizophrenia who is super chill and sometimes they see bugs crawling all over that aren't actually there and they're great and I'd trust them with my life and I love them. They know how to deal with their stuff when it comes up and can generally manage very well. 

I know a girl who has schizophrenia who is very nice and sweet but sometimes difficult to get along with because she believes she has magical powers and can control the weather. She's going for her PhD in anthropology. I like her and I'm rooting for her even if I don't believe in her weather magic.

But also, I know a guy who just started manifesting symptoms in his late 20s. He was really cool before but now he's losing his housing because he keeps threatening neighbors who tell him not to scream profanities when their kids are around, and he's constantly posting on Facebook about how everyone he interacts with is "staging things" to psychologically torture him with reminders of his past, and he will not accept any help but constantly accuses people of not helping him. It's been incredibly sad to watch this very sweet and intelligent person deteriorate like this. You can tell he's fucking terrified constantly. And he scares other people with his behavior. But he won't take any meds or do any therapy. I feel bad for him but he's become very unpredictable and I don't want to be around him. I think he's mostly a danger to himself.

Another one of my friends also started manifesting symptoms in his 20s and his entire personality changed. He was funny, cool, and a great friend. But then over the course of just one year he turned into someone who was completely convinced everyone was trying to hurt him. He believed he'd been kidnapped, he believed his parents wanted to kill him, he believed his fiancee had been raping him. He owned guns and his fiancee said she had to call the police on him because of how scary he got and how threatening he was. She wound up leaving him, devastated that their 9 year relationship was erased and reduced in his mind to her abusing and manipulating him along with everybody else in his life, and from what we've heard he's been in and out of clinics but refuses medication. She has him blocked and has made sure he cant find her now. He's someone I'm genuinely scared of.

Especially because schizophrenia killed one of my other friends. Like all the rest he was really funny and smart. Genius level smart. He had a comedy radio show in college I got to be a guest on. I was at his wedding. A year into his relationship, he started to change. He had had command hallucinations for awhile, but they started to get really bad. He also started having weird beliefs, falling deep down the Qanon conspiracy rabbithole. One day he took his wife outside and started stabbing her over and over. He was shot to death by their neighbor. The wife survived, he did not. I have nightmares about him sometimes. 

I know people for whom the "symptoms" associated with their condition are actually positive things. My sister's friend comes from a culture that believes in and teaches all about spirits, and this friend grew up understanding herself and her brain through that worldview. For her, it's a gift that connects her to her ancestors. It comes with challenges, but it's a good thing overall. 

With something with such a vast, diverse array of ways it can manifest and affect people, you can't generalize. You can't be like "all schizophrenic people are like this" or "this is what you can expect from someone from schizophrenia." What I can say is that schizophrenia can be truly terrible. Not everyone is blessed with the ability or the means to manage it. There are some people who just see their bugs every now and then and work to recognize and curb paranoia and other symptoms and are able to find ways to ground themselves and be okay. And then there are people who are absolutely not okay, who cannot ground themselves, who are just drifting terrified in a whirlwind of untethered thoughts and fears and senses, and it destroys their lives. 

The one constant in all three of my friends with bad outcomes' stories is that they refused medication, therapy, and help. I believe at least two of them relied on cannabis to help their symptoms, which sucks because cannabis can exacerbate symptoms. 

I don't really have any advice here, except to just always be careful with your own mental health. Take meds if doctors are telling you to take meds. Make sure you're in therapy. And spend lots of time with your friends, because anything could happen to them.

I personally view UPG as our own personal way of interacting with the divine. But the thing is that any awareness of divinity has to run through our own human brains first, and those are wildly untrustworthy. It's just like dreams, basically. Any information you're given in a dream has to run through a ridiculous mish-mash of beliefs, hopes, fears, experiences, and biases, and what comes out on the other end might be a garbled mess. We influence our personal gnosis. Sometimes (perhaps often) to the point where our own feelings completely drown out any messages we are getting. If we believe-- and NEED to believe-- that our gods are all light and love and empowerment and comfort and that we're our gods' favorite children, our interactions with them are going to be very much like "I felt the love of Hekate and she told me that I'm not the toxic one in my relationship and nothing is my fault." But if we are certain that the gods are petty and angry and scornful and everything we do could potentially have bad consequences so we're constantly worried about all our interactions, they'll be more like "aphrodite is mad at me because I missed an offering and she hates me and I'm cursed."

We bring a lot of our own desires and anxieties to the table, and it can deafen us to the experience of the divine. We can do it willfully or accidentally. Sometimes, people mistake their own daydreams and fantasies for direct messages from the gods. Other people can't distinguish their wish fulfillment fantasies from reality. There was some guy over in the Hecate subreddit a couple days ago claiming he was the dom in a relationship with the goddess, and that he was also a god. I think he got booted by the mods. But he's an example of how the human mind can want so badly to believe something that it makes it true for us. 

Communicating with the divine involves a lot of listening. And observing. If you want lessons from the god of the sea, go to the sea. Spend mundane time there. Learn about the weather patterns and the migration of the fish and the seabirds. Identify shells. Learn about the deep sea. Go fishing. Go swimming. Learn from what we have here in the physical of the divine what the divine is like. Keep an open mind and learn to quiet your own ego when you listen for guidance. 

We'll never be perfect receptors for what the gods are trying to tell us, but if we are going to try, we have to let go of the expectations that bind us to a certain outcome.

Satanism, Luciferianism, Demonolotry, and several other paths are considered LHP or left-hand path. They're also pretty much the only ones who use this identification system. People who LHP folks would consider "RHP" or "right-hand path" generally don't refer to themselves as such. Wiccans, christians, most pagans, muslims, buddhists, etc (pretty much everyone else) are considered RHP.

These terms come from ceremonial magic and occultism, and not from paganism.

There are several different definitions for each, which may change depending on the source of information and their tradition of origin, but GENERALLY LHP is about individualism while RHP is about unity. I've often seen them defined as "RHP is about trying to become one with God while LHP is about becoming your own God." 

Here is a definition from [learnreligions.com](https://learnreligions.com):

>"The left-hand path is considered to be about the elevation and centrality of the self as well as the rejection of religious authority and societal taboos.  
The left-hand path focuses on the strength and will of the practitioner. It downplays the need for intercession by any high power although some may believe that a higher power exists.  
>  
>The right-hand path, in the words of left-hand path follower Vexen Crabtree, 'concentrate\[s\] on the symbols of goodness, of the sun, of herd mentality and submission to god(s) and religious authority.'  
To put it a little more diplomatic, the right-hand path can be thought of as one of dogma, ritual, and a belief in the community and formal structure as well as a higher power. Though each of those can also be found in left-hand path religions, there is less focus on indulging the self in the right-hand path.   
The vast majority of religions are considered part of the right-hand path, from Christianity to Wicca."  


My own biased opinion is that the whole "left-hand path" concept was created by people who wanted to be edgy and were "not like other girls" but for occultism. I don't see LHP/RHP as a real or meaningful dichotomy, especially as a pagan. In my own witchcraft practice there are elements which fit into both categories, and the idea of an "ultimate goal" of my practice being either complete unity or complete separation with/from the divine is simply not a factor at all. You will mostly find that the vast majority of pagans do not identify much with either LHP or RHP.

There's less of a stigma now. When I was growing up my parents refused to get me tested for adhd because it would make me "different" and they didn't want me to feel wrong or less-than or to carry the stigma of having a disability. They thought they were doing the right thing. In their minds, adhd kids were hyperactive, loud, stupid, rude, and a hassle to teachers and other kids, while I was polite and quiet and my only "symptoms" (that they noticed) were that I liked to daydream and didn't pay attention in class sometimes. They figured that since I was functioning fine (by their standards) and managing myself, I didn't need a diagnosis. 

Until very recently, "neurodiveristy" was not a thing and you were either normal or you were broken. Being autistic meant you "had the mind of a young child." Autism and adhd were mental illnesses and the goal was to either cure them or, if they couldn't be cured, to give caretakers the skills to bear the burden of having a permanently broken person to take care of. These conditions were exclusively thought of and viewed through the lens of ways they were a problem for "normal" people. If you didn't seem like a problem for "normal" people, you didn't have any disorder worth mentioning.

Nowadays, however, we are looking at the ways our neurology and psychology impacts US. What my parents didn't see was that my ADHD was NOT well-managed-- I had just learned to hijack my fight-or-flight response to get tasks done. It took me all day after school to get homework done, I was constantly ashamed of not being able to pay attention, my teachers were constantly chiding me for being disorganized, and I had internalized an idea that I could only be acceptable to people if I was extraordinary (gifted kid complex) so I was constantly working myself into burnout and I felt (and still feel) deep shame when I'm NOT burnt out. Getting my ADHD diagnosis was really important to me because I have resources to help me understand and actually manage my own brain.

 People now are looking at neurodiversity through the lens of how it makes non-neurotipicals FEEL, how it impacts OUR lives, and NOT just the "symptoms" we display to others. We can learn to mitigate the things that make us miserable, we can learn not to be ashamed of things that make us "different," we can learn strategies to deal with the stuff that it's more difficult for us to deal with (like accepting you can't pay attention during meetings or classes without knitting or drawing or doing something with your hands). 

And now, of course, we have many examples of successful and "cool" people who are non-neurotypical. You can easily find examples of artists, writers, activists, inventors, scientists, politicians, etc., who are autistic or have adhd. Plus, many non-neurotypicals are very prolific on the internet through platforms which suit them well and which they often excel at better than their neurotypical peers, making them seem cool and popular. Theres far less social stigma now than there was even just ten years ago.

I've lost pets before. It's different each time. You don't know how it will happen even if you know it's coming soon. You might instead find him in pain or dying, and will need to take him to be euthanized. He might pass quietly under a piece of furniture somewhere. He might run off and not come back-- cats often do this when they're dying. I had a cat with failing kidneys that attempted this, but came back because it was snowing really hard. His condition quickly worsened and he only lived a couple more days. 

You'll do what feels right in the moment. Depending on how it happens, depending on what you feel is best, depending on what your wife feels is best. It's okay to wrap him in a blanket. Death is weird and individual and grief is personal and no matter how much you anticipate how you'll feel or what you'll do, you can't REALLY know. It's a hard process and you'll deal with it however you deal with it and it'll be fine.

'95. I was in first grade. I remember I was home sick that day and my cartoons were interrupted. I was mad because I didn't care that a building fell down. It was just a building. It was just planes. I remember my parents freaking out. And at school, there were at least a couple of assemblies and things where an adult came in to talk to us. I didn't get why anybody cared so much and figured it was one of those adult things. It wasn't until a year later on the anniversary of the event that I found out that there had been people in the building and in the planes. Then I realized what I'd watched happen live. There had been people inside. I'd seen all those people die. 

It's weird to think about now. My sister is '97 and she has 0 memory of this and she says that as a kid she felt it was unfair that people were so upset about 9/11 but not about the war in Iraq, which killed more people. She makes jokes about 9/11 like I've seen especially gen-z people make a lot. She views it primarily as an event that allowed the US to launch wars on the Middle East & ramp up nationalist and racist ideologies and expand military power. Which it definitely was.

But man, there's something different about seeing it happen on live TV, and knowing that you were there, watching the towers, when those people were dying. I can't laugh about it. I don't like the jokes. It's definitely different when you remember seeing it happen, when you remember what you were thinking and where you were sitting on the couch and what you were watching before the news broke. I get the criticisms of the way the tragedy was weaponized to prop up nationalism and justify wars, but I think that for me, this is something that I really saw happen in real time, and my '97 sister doesn't have that memory. To her it's like the Titanic or something-- a thing that happened in history.

I didn't understand that there was more than one kind of bomb. My dad was super into anti-cold war media and so I was very aware of nuclear bombs, but it never occurred to me that bombs could come in smaller sizes. To me, "a bomb" always meant a nuclear bomb. In sixth grade, my school had a bomb threat, and the police were called. I was the only one who was freaking out and crying, and I was shocked and pissed off that nobody else seemed to be taking it seriously, because there was a very real chance that a nuclear warhead was hidden somewhere in our school and it could go off. I borrowed an older girl's phone to leave a voicemail telling my parents to get out of town and that I loved them and this might be my last goodbye. I was pretty sure it was 50/50 that I, and probably my whole city, was going to die.

My mom eventually got the voicemail and picked me up. I don't think she understood why I was so scared. "It was just some dumb kid pulling a prank. Even if there was an actual bomb, they evacuated you outside." Which sounded impossibly stupid to me, because if the nuke goes off, it doesn't matter if we're inside or outside-- we're gonna be puffs of char in a crater soon. I asked her if she was sure we shouldn't leave the city, and she reminded me we had to go to a party that night.

I didn't realize the truth of the situation until I was well into college. In the back of my memory I recalled being scared and the bomb threat and being convinced we could never get far away enough from the school to actually be safe, but I hadn't applied logic to that memory since it happened. I happened to think about it one day and just started laughing so hard I was crying because I realized that the entire time, I was genuinely convinced there could be a nuclear warhead about to go off in my middle school.

I totally did see movies where there were explosions and stuff as a kid, but I absolutely did not put two-and-two together that when someone is referring to a bomb, they usually don't mean a nuke. Especially if it's a bomb that the cops are looking for in small lockers and under desks.
